questions.question: What is the difference between unit testing, integration testing and end-to-end testing?

definition.text: Unit, integration, and end-to-end tests examine different boundaries.

motivation.whyIntroduced: A single testing style cannot economically detect every defect. Fast isolated checks catch incorrect calculations, integration tests catch errors at system boundaries, and realistic end-to-end checks catch failures in user journeys. Teams combine them to balance execution speed, confidence, and maintenance cost.
motivation.historicalNote: Testing terminology predates Angular. Angular TestBed supports component/service isolation; API contract and database tests cover integrations; browser tools such as Playwright can exercise real user flows. The testing pyramid is a useful heuristic rather than a mandatory percentage formula.

problemSolved.before: A checkout team only tests a complete purchase with a slow browser suite; a minor calculation error is found late and is difficult to localize.
problemSolved.after: Pure checkout calculations have fast unit tests, checkout-to-API behavior has integration/contract tests, and a small number of critical journeys run end to end.
benefits: Quicker feedback for straightforward defects
Focused diagnosis when tests fail
Coverage for boundary and browser behavior
Reduced dependence on brittle full-browser tests

characteristics: Unit tests focus on one small behavior with controlled dependencies.
Integration tests verify cooperation between real components such as API and persistence, with a clearly stated boundary.
End-to-end tests execute user-visible workflows through a deployed or locally running application.
A flaky test gives inconsistent results and must be investigated instead of repeatedly ignored.
Coverage percentage is evidence about executed code, not proof of correctness or good assertions.

simpleAnalogy.title: Inspecting a restaurant order
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A unit check confirms a recipe measures correctly; integration checks the kitchen and order ticket agree; end-to-end checks a diner can order, pay, and receive the intended dish.

industryExample.scenario: An online shop must calculate item totals, save orders, and complete a customer checkout journey.
industryExample.implementation: Unit-test the money calculation, integration-test checkout API persistence using a test database, and use a Playwright browser test for product-to-order confirmation. Use sandbox payments and fixture products.
industryExample.businessImpact: The team detects arithmetic, API-contract, and browser-navigation regressions with different layers of evidence.
industryExample.importantConstraint: A browser test alone cannot prove transaction atomicity, and mocked integration tests do not replace security and persistence checks.

useCases: HTTP services tested with a fake backend
Critical user journeys such as registration and checkout

steps: Developer changes checkout fee logic
Unit tests validate a pure total calculation
Integration test verifies checkout API creates correct order rows
E2E test opens storefront and completes sandbox checkout
CI records failures and blocks unsafe release
Team investigates the earliest failing layer to localize cause

pitfalls: Relying only on happy-path browser tests misses edge cases and creates slow diagnosis.
Mocking every boundary in an integration test makes it another unit test.
A passing test can assert the wrong thing; assertion quality matters more than count.
Tests tied to implementation details break unnecessarily during refactoring.
Production payment guarantees require backend invariants and independent failure testing.
whenNotToUse: Do not use E2E tests to exhaustively test every arithmetic branch.
Do not treat 100% line coverage as proof of safety.
Never run real payment or patient-data operations in automated demonstrations.

alternatives.bestFor: Deterministic calculation or validation rules
alternatives.tradeoff: Cannot demonstrate API or browser integration

alternatives.name: Angular TestBed test
alternatives.bestFor: Component and service behavior with providers

alternatives.tradeoff: Slower, requires controlled infrastructure

alternatives.name: Playwright E2E
alternatives.bestFor: User-critical browser workflow
alternatives.tradeoff: Most expensive and more sensitive to environment

testing.strategy: Use layered tests appropriate to the risk: pure logic, Angular TestBed with controlled providers, HttpTestingController for API behavior, API authorization tests, and Playwright for critical user workflows. Test both success and failure and ensure test data is synthetic.

questions.topic: Angular TestBed, component fixtures and service mocks
questions.question: How do you test an Angular component and mock a service dependency?

definition.text: TestBed creates Angular components with replaceable testing dependencies.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Components often depend on APIs, auth state, or configuration. Real network calls make component tests slow and unpredictable. Angular TestBed can construct the component with test-controlled providers and a fixture so tests can assert real template output and interactions.
motivation.historicalNote: Angular TestBed is the standard Angular testing utility and works with testing runners such as Vitest. Standalone components can be included in TestBed imports. Replacing an injected service using providers is preferable to changing the component to accommodate tests.

problemSolved.before: A clinician worklist component calls a live backend during every test and fails when the service or network is unavailable.
problemSolved.after: The test replaces the data service with a deterministic fake and verifies the rendered patient-count summary and user interaction.
benefits: Repeatable component behavior without a backend
Assertions on real Angular template rendering
Controlled success, empty and failure inputs
Clearer separation between UI responsibility and API responsibility

characteristics: TestBed.configureTestingModule configures an Angular testing injector.
Standalone components are commonly placed in the test imports list.
ComponentFixture gives access to the component, debug element and native DOM.
A useValue fake overrides the service dependency for this test scope.
fixture.detectChanges or fixture.whenStable supports view update and async stabilization depending on the test.

simpleAnalogy.title: Training simulator for a pilot
simpleAnalogy.explanation: The cockpit uses a simulated air-traffic feed while the instructor verifies how instruments and controls respond. The interface is real; the outside system is controlled.

industryExample.scenario: A scheduling dashboard displays how many appointments a clinician has today.
industryExample.implementation: Inject an AppointmentService and in the component test override it with a fake returning a fixed list. Use TestBed to render the standalone component and assert the displayed count.
industryExample.businessImpact: A regression in the worklist UI is caught without relying on patient APIs or exposing sensitive records.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Mock-based UI tests do not verify backend authorization; that must be covered by separate API and security tests.

useCases: Display counts and lists from injected services
Test accessibility labels and empty states

steps: TestBed configures the standalone component and fake provider
Angular injector supplies fake AppointmentService
Fixture creates component and renders template
Test triggers change detection or awaits stability
Test queries DOM and asserts accessible content
API contract behavior is tested separately using HTTP test tools

The standalone component is declared in imports, not declarations.

pitfalls: Putting a standalone component in declarations instead of imports.
Mocking a different provider token than the component actually injects.
Asserting component fields but forgetting to verify the user-visible DOM.
Assuming detectChanges settles every pending asynchronous operation.
Accidentally allowing real HTTP calls to leak into unit/component tests.
whenNotToUse: Do not use a UI fake as evidence that backend authorization works.
Do not inject real patient data into local test fixtures or source control.
Do not test private implementation methods when public behavior is testable.

alternatives.tradeoff: Does not validate rendered HTML

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

definition.text: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions afterward.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Knowing who a requester is does not tell the system what they are allowed to access. If the same rule is applied to every signed-in user, administrators, clinicians, and customers could see or change each other’s records. Keeping identity verification distinct from resource authorization prevents that mistake.
motivation.historicalNote: Identity and access control are established computer-security concepts. Modern web apps frequently use OIDC for login and OAuth-based tokens for API access, but token possession alone does not grant universal privileges. The server must evaluate subject, resource, action, and context.

problemSolved.before: Any signed-in SaaS employee can open any organization’s invoices because the API checks only whether a session exists.
problemSolved.after: The API authenticates the caller and then checks tenant membership plus invoice-view permission for the specific invoice.
benefits: Clear separation between identity and permissions
Reduced cross-user and cross-tenant exposure
Auditable allow/deny decisions
Consistent enforcement even if browser code is modified

characteristics: Authentication answers who the requester is; it uses credentials or a valid session.
Authorization answers whether this subject can do this action on this resource.
Client-side guards and hidden buttons are usability controls, not access control boundaries.
Least privilege grants only the permissions needed for the task.
Server-side policies must verify tenant ownership and resource scope, not only role names.

simpleAnalogy.title: Office badge and restricted door
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A badge scanner establishes that you work in the building. A separate door policy decides whether you may enter the finance records room.

industryExample.scenario: A user belongs to Tenant A and tries to view invoices belonging to Tenant B.
industryExample.implementation: After authenticating the session, the backend checks a tenant-scoped invoice-view permission and verifies that the invoice belongs to the tenant identified by the authorized context. Angular may hide the link but does not make the final access decision.
industryExample.businessImpact: Cross-tenant invoice data remains protected even when a user edits requests in browser DevTools.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Never trust a tenant ID, role or resource-owner flag sent by the browser without backend validation.

steps: Browser sends an authenticated request for invoice INV-7
Backend validates the session or bearer credentials
Backend resolves the caller and trusted tenant context
Policy checks invoice-view permission on INV-7
Repository constrains lookup by authorized tenant
Backend returns data if allowed, otherwise 403 or an appropriate privacy-preserving response

explanation: The function accepts a verified principal, not a user-controlled request body field.
Both permission and membership are necessary; checking only one would be incomplete.
The database query must also be tenant-scoped to avoid retrieving unauthorized resources.
Angular can reuse a permission read model for button visibility, but backend decisions remain authoritative.

projectExperience.example: In the SaaS portfolio project, I would write an invoice API that derives the subject from a verified session, enforces tenant-scoped policies, and tests attempted cross-tenant reads.

pitfalls: Treating a valid JWT as permission to perform any action.
Trusting roles or tenant IDs supplied directly by the client.
Checking permission but forgetting record ownership or organization scope.
Assuming Angular route guards protect API endpoints.
Logging credentials, access tokens or sensitive invoice payloads during denials.
whenNotToUse: Never rely solely on UI hiding or client-side route guards for security.
Never assume authentication means administrator authorization.
Never trust client-origin tenant membership claims without server verification.

alternatives.name: Resource ownership checks
alternatives.bestFor: Per-record access such as account holder or treating clinician
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires secure identity-to-record mapping

alternatives.name: Capability-based access
alternatives.bestFor: Narrow delegated operations with explicit scopes
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires safe capability issuance, expiration and revocation

questions.topic: Cross-site scripting and Angular template security
questions.question: What is XSS, and how does Angular help protect applications from unsafe content?

definition.text: XSS executes attacker-controlled scripts within another user’s browser.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Applications render values supplied by other users, APIs and content systems. If untrusted text becomes executable HTML or JavaScript, an attacker can run actions in the victim’s browser context. Safe rendering and contextual sanitization prevent this class of injection in common template operations.
motivation.historicalNote: Browsers historically trusted page scripts and dynamic HTML. Frameworks such as Angular treat template values as untrusted by default: interpolation escapes values and Angular sanitizes appropriate bound HTML and URLs. Protection is contextual; browser DOM APIs and bypass methods can circumvent safeguards.

problemSolved.before: A support-ticket portal assigns a user-submitted issue description directly to element.innerHTML, allowing malicious markup to execute or mutate the page.
problemSolved.after: Angular renders plain text through interpolation and uses contextual sanitization when HTML binding is truly necessary; server input policy and CSP provide additional layers.
benefits: Untrusted text displays as text rather than executable markup
Framework-managed security contexts for common bindings
Less manual DOM manipulation
Defense in depth with Trusted Types and CSP

characteristics: Angular interpolation escapes untrusted values inserted as text.
Binding HTML via [innerHTML] uses HTML sanitization, not unrestricted execution.
Resource URLs that could load executable code cannot be made safe through generic sanitization.
Direct ElementRef.nativeElement.innerHTML and third-party DOM manipulation can bypass Angular protection.
bypassSecurityTrustHtml marks content trusted and is unsafe on attacker-controlled data.

simpleAnalogy.title: Writing on a public noticeboard
simpleAnalogy.explanation: If a visitor can paste instructions that the building staff automatically obeys, a simple note becomes dangerous. Safe rendering treats visitor content as writing to display, not commands to execute.

industryExample.scenario: A hospital support portal displays ticket descriptions written by staff, including copied HTML-like characters.
industryExample.implementation: Bind the issue description with Angular interpolation so tags are displayed as text. If an approved rich-text requirement exists, sanitize via a reviewed pipeline and Angular security contexts; forbid arbitrary script-capable content.
industryExample.businessImpact: The support page can show user-entered text without interpreting it as executable browser content.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Healthcare privacy also requires server-side authorization, safe logs, retention controls and CSP; Angular escaping alone does not secure medical data.

useCases: User comments or support ticket descriptions
Product review snippets and marketplace listings
External API data rendered in templates
Rich-text display with approved sanitization policies

steps: User submits a fictional support note containing HTML-like text
API stores the note under an authorized record
Angular receives an untrusted string from the API
Template interpolation creates visible text, not executable markup
Browser displays the literal text safely
Security tests verify no injected DOM nodes or actions appear

pitfalls: Using bypassSecurityTrustHtml on untrusted text disables a major safety boundary.
Direct DOM APIs bypass Angular template sanitization protections.
An escaped string used later in a script or URL context may still be unsafe.
Client sanitization does not replace server permission checks.
A trusted-looking API response is not automatically safe to render as raw HTML.
whenNotToUse: Never compile untrusted user strings into Angular templates.
Never trust arbitrary user HTML with bypassSecurityTrustHtml.
Never build script, style or resource URLs from unvalidated user input.

alternatives.bestFor: Editor-generated rich text with constrained node types
alternatives.tradeoff: More application code and schema maintenance

alternatives.name: Direct DOM APIs
alternatives.bestFor: Rare integrations with trusted libraries
alternatives.tradeoff: High risk without strong sanitization and code review

Literal angle brackets appear without created image/script elements.
Component renders a valid empty note area.
Reviewed sanitization removes unsafe markup before rendering.

negativeCases: Supply markup containing an inline event handler and assert no executable element appears.
Try a URL-based injection in an unrelated link-binding path and verify it is rejected or sanitized.

questions.question: An API call returns HTTP 401. How would you trace the issue using browser DevTools, the network tab and backend logs?

definition.text: A 401 response indicates missing or invalid authentication credentials.

motivation.whyIntroduced: A failed request may be caused by an expired session, missing credentials, misconfigured interceptor, incorrect API origin, clock skew, or identity-provider configuration. Debugging should distinguish where the failure occurs rather than adding retries or assuming a frontend bug.
motivation.historicalNote: HTTP 401 is defined by HTTP authentication semantics. Its meaning differs from 403: a request lacking valid authentication typically yields 401, while authenticated access denied by permissions often yields 403. Implementations vary; backend logs and request IDs provide the final evidence.

problemSolved.before: A developer sees 401, blindly retries the API repeatedly and exposes tokens in browser console logs while trying to debug.
problemSolved.after: The team identifies the exact failing request, checks whether credentials are attached without copying secrets, correlates the request ID with server logs, validates token/session conditions and fixes the actual configuration or session state.
benefits: Faster root-cause isolation
Safer handling of tokens and user data
Correct distinction between login failure and permission denial
Verifiable fix rather than masking symptoms

characteristics: HTTP 401 generally means valid authentication was not supplied or accepted.
HTTP 403 usually means the authenticated request is not permitted, subject to API privacy choices.
Network DevTools reveals request URL, method, status and whether authentication was sent.
Interceptors may attach credentials or transform errors and should not erase diagnostic context.
Server correlation IDs connect browser failures with backend and identity-system logs.

simpleAnalogy.title: Train station ticket gate
simpleAnalogy.explanation: If a ticket scanner rejects a ticket, check whether the ticket exists, is readable, and is still valid before blaming the train schedule. A reference number helps staff locate the exact attempt.

industryExample.scenario: A customer can open a read-only dashboard, but fetching the transaction list returns 401 after the session expires.
industryExample.implementation: Record the request ID and status in DevTools, inspect whether the request used the expected credentials without exposing their value, check session expiry and origin/cookie settings, then correlate the backend log to the auth middleware denial. Redirect to a safe re-authentication flow only when appropriate.
industryExample.businessImpact: The incident is resolved with reliable session handling and without sending customer credentials to logs or repeatedly replaying account requests.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Do not automatically retry sensitive writes after authentication failure; a successful payment must not be assumed or duplicated.

useCases: Expired access token or session cookie
Missing Authorization header from interceptor configuration
Cross-origin credential or cookie SameSite configuration error

steps: User triggers transaction list fetch
Angular HttpClient sends request through configured interceptors
Browser Network tab records request URL, headers presence and 401
Safe client logging records method/path/status/request ID only
Backend access logs correlate the request ID with authentication middleware
Team fixes session renewal or credential configuration and verifies a successful new request

codeExample.runtime: Modern Angular standalone TypeScript teaching sample. Vitest examples require a configured test runner; Angular TestBed examples require the Angular test environment. Examples must be tested in a configured Angular workspace before production use.
explanation: The interceptor only logs a safe diagnostic subset of 401 failures, then rethrows the original error.
URL pathname extraction intentionally removes query-string secrets but does not guarantee path segments are nonsensitive.
The example does not attempt silent refresh; that requires a separate, carefully tested session policy.
Network tab and server correlation logs determine whether cookies, credentials, expiration or configuration caused the failure.

projectExperience.example: In the banking sample app, I would expire a synthetic user session, reproduce a 401, capture redacted request metadata, correlate a test backend auth log and verify the re-login behavior.

pitfalls: Logging Authorization headers or entire error objects that may contain sensitive data.
Confusing 401 with authorization 403 and applying the wrong remediation.
Automatically retrying an unsafe write without idempotency and outcome confirmation.
Swallowing errors in an interceptor and leaving UI loading forever.
Assuming CORS failures always appear as ordinary HTTP 401 responses in browser JavaScript.
whenNotToUse: Never paste live tokens, cookies or patient identifiers into tickets or logs.
Never retry payment writes automatically after an uncertain outcome.
Never use blanket 401-to-login redirects for public endpoints without a documented policy.

alternatives.name: Browser Network tab
alternatives.bestFor: Immediate request/response and credential-presence inspection
alternatives.tradeoff: May not reveal why server rejected credentials

alternatives.name: Correlation IDs in backend logs
alternatives.bestFor: Find authentication rejection reason and middleware path
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires redaction, access control and logging setup

alternatives.name: HttpTestingController test
alternatives.bestFor: Deterministically test interceptor error behavior
alternatives.tradeoff: Cannot diagnose deployed identity or cookie configuration

alternatives.name: End-to-end expired-session test
alternatives.bestFor: Exercise browser-to-API authentication behavior
alternatives.tradeoff: Slower and requires controlled identity test environment

testing.strategy: Use layered tests appropriate to the risk: pure logic, Angular TestBed with controlled providers, HttpTestingController for API behavior, API authorization tests, and Playwright for critical user workflows. Test both success and failure and ensure test data is synthetic.

testCases.expected: 401 is reported without logging credentials; UI offers safe reauthentication.
Transaction request succeeds and no 401 diagnostic is emitted.
No misleading 401 diagnosis is recorded; access-denied UI handles permissions.
Client and server diagnostics agree on a synthetic correlation identifier.

negativeCases: Simulate a 401 with a secret query string and verify telemetry does not include it.
Simulate repeated 401 responses and verify no infinite retry loop or token leak occurs.

beginner: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
intermediate: How do you test HttpInterceptorFn with HttpTestingController?
advanced: How do you diagnose cross-origin cookie failures and concurrent session refreshes?
expert: How would you design secure authentication observability and incident response across regions and tenants?

answer.finalTakeaway: Trace the exact request and trusted server evidence without leaking credentials.

learningOutcomes: Explain diagnosing http 401 in angular applications in clear technical language with an industry example.
Adapt the supplied code in an appropriate Angular or TypeScript project.
Test success and failure behavior and explain the relevant security or reliability boundary.
